annotations.description: With a hand containing no 1-drop creatures and a curve starting at 2 mana (Deep-Cavern Bat), choosing to play first means drawing one fewer card. The hand has Kaito (4 mana) and two Deep-Cavern Bats but limited early pressure and no turn-1 play. On the draw, the extra card could help find additional lands or action. However, going first does allow Turn 2 Deep-Cavern Bat to strip a card before the opponent develops, which is a legitimate tempo play. This is close but the hand's mana base (Island, Swamp, Multiversal Passage, Soulstone Sanctuary) is a bit awkward and an extra draw could help smooth things out.

annotations.betterLine: Going first is defensible with Turn 2 Deep-Cavern Bat for hand disruption, but going on the draw for the extra card with this somewhat clunky hand was worth considering.

annotations.description: Playing Multiversal Passage on turn 1 when there are no turn-1 plays wastes the flexibility of this dual-purpose land. With Island, Swamp, and Soulstone Sanctuary also in hand, playing a basic land first preserves Multiversal Passage's ability to fill whatever color gap emerges later. The hand wants B on turn 2 for Deep-Cavern Bat and UB by turn 4 for Kaito — playing Swamp turn 1 achieves the same curve while keeping Multiversal Passage flexible.
annotations.betterLine: Play Swamp turn 1, preserving Multiversal Passage's flexibility to fill whatever color is needed later in the game.

The redundant Island is less valuable than a second Swamp given the hand composition.

annotations.description: Playing Swamp instead of Island means the player cannot cast Deep-Cavern Bat on turn 2 (which costs {1}{B} and could be cast with Multiversal Passage choosing Swamp + Island for the {1}). Wait - Multiversal Passage was already chosen as a basic land type when it entered. Let me reconsider. The Multiversal Passage chose a basic land type on entry. We don't know what type was chosen. If it was chosen as Swamp, then playing Island would give access to both {B} and {U}, enabling Deep-Cavern Bat (1B) with either land providing the generic, AND keeping Floodpits Drowner (1U) as an option. If Multiversal Passage was chosen as Island, then playing Swamp enables Deep-Cavern Bat but not Floodpits Drowner. Playing Island would mean two Islands and no black mana. So the choice depends on what Multiversal Passage was set to. Given MiMo paid 2 life (went from 20 to 18) to have it enter untapped, and the hand has Deep-Cavern Bat and Kaito requiring black, it was likely chosen as Swamp. With Multiversal Passage as Swamp, playing Island would give {B} + {U} enabling both Deep-Cavern Bat AND holding up Floodpits Drowner as options. Playing Swamp gives {B}{B} which only enables Deep-Cavern Bat but not Floodpits Drowner. Island would have been more flexible, keeping open the option to flash in Floodpits Drowner if the opponent plays a threatening creature.
annotations.actionTaken: Played Swamp as the second land, resulting in two black sources but no blue mana.
annotations.betterLine: Play Island to have access to both black (from Multiversal Passage likely set to Swamp) and blue mana, enabling both Deep-Cavern Bat and keeping Floodpits Drowner as a flash option.

annotations.description: With 3 lands available (Multiversal Passage, Swamp, and the Island about to be played), MiMo could cast Deep-Cavern Bat (1B) this turn to look at the opponent's hand and potentially exile a key card. Playing Island instead of Soulstone Sanctuary is fine, but the real issue is not following up by casting Deep-Cavern Bat. However, looking at the choices more carefully, the decision is specifically about which card to play from the four options. Deep-Cavern Bat costs {1}{B} and MiMo has Swamp + Multiversal Passage (chosen as a basic land type - we don't know which type). If Multiversal Passage was chosen as Island or Swamp, then with Swamp + Multiversal Passage they might have the mana. But they also have Floodpits Drowner on the battlefield (untapped 2/1 with vigilance). Playing Island and then casting Deep-Cavern Bat with Swamp + Island/Passage would work if they have {1}{B}. Actually, the choices show Island AND Deep-Cavern Bat as separate options - they could potentially play Island AND then cast Deep-Cavern Bat. But since this is the chosen action (Island over Deep-Cavern Bat), and the game shows the turn then passes to Qwen3 Timmy, it seems MiMo only played the Island and didn't cast Deep-Cavern Bat. Deep-Cavern Bat on turn 3 is a strong tempo play - it provides hand information, can exile a threat, and has evasion + lifelink. Missing this deployment is a real missed opportunity.

annotations.betterLine: Play Island, then cast Deep-Cavern Bat using Swamp + one other land to see opponent's hand and exile a key card like Spider Manifestation or Nature's Rhythm

annotations.description: Playing Soulstone Sanctuary instead of Deep-Cavern Bat is suboptimal. With 2 mana available (Multiversal Passage + Swamp, or Island + Swamp), MiMo could cast Deep-Cavern Bat to see the opponent's hand, potentially exile a key card like Nature's Rhythm or Craterhoof Behemoth, gain incremental lifelink damage, and still have the land drop available next turn. Deep-Cavern Bat is a tempo play that provides critical information and disruption while also adding a flying attacker alongside Floodpits Drowner. Playing Soulstone Sanctuary (a colorless land that enters untapped) doesn't enable anything meaningful this turn that couldn't wait - the 4-mana activation is expensive and the extra mana isn't needed immediately. The bat gives information, disruption, evasive pressure, and lifelink.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Deep-Cavern Bat using Swamp + Island/Multiversal Passage to scout opponent's hand and exile a key spell, then play Soulstone Sanctuary next turn. This provides hand disruption, a flying lifelink attacker, and still allows the land drop later.

With Floodpits Drowner attacking unblocked, Ninjutsu for {1}{U}{B} would deploy a 3/4 hexproof threat that generates emblems and card advantage. annotations.description: MiMo Gramps used Shoot the Sheriff to destroy the opponent's Llanowar Elves instead of one of their own creatures that was a valid target. Shoot the Sheriff says 'Destroy target non-outlaw creature' — it can target any non-outlaw creature on either side. However, looking at the context more carefully: MiMo Gramps is the one casting Shoot the Sheriff, so they're choosing what to kill. Llanowar Elves is the opponent's mana dork, while Floodpits Drowner and Deep-Cavern Bat are MiMo's own creatures. Killing the opponent's Llanowar Elves removes their mana acceleration when they're already at 11 life with only 2 lands. However, this is being cast during MiMo's own combat phase, which means MiMo spent mana on removal during their own attack step rather than before or after combat. More importantly, the Deep-Cavern Bat is tapped (likely attacked or just entered), and Floodpits Drowner could have attacked. The real question is whether killing Llanowar Elves was the right target — and it actually seems reasonable since it denies the opponent mana. But casting a removal spell during your own combat phase is unusual timing. Actually, re-reading: the opponent has Spider-Sense in graveyard, so no counterspell threat. Killing Llanowar Elves to deny mana when the opponent is at 11 life and only has 2 lands is actually a reasonable play to keep them constrained. This seems fine.
annotations.actionTaken: Targeted Llanowar Elves with Shoot the Sheriff during own combat phase
annotations.betterLine: This is actually reasonable — denying the opponent's only mana acceleration when they're land-light keeps them constrained. The timing during combat is slightly awkward but the target choice is defensible.
